title: WAS SARAH WRONG TO GIVE HAGAR TO ABRAHAM? THE STORY IS MORE DISTURBING THAN MANY SERMONS ADMIT.
paragraphs: WAS SARAH WRONG TO GIVE HAGAR TO ABRAHAM? THE STORY IS MORE DISTURBING THAN MANY SERMONS ADMIT.

She was a wife desperate for God's promise. Hagar was an enslaved woman who had little power to refuse. Abraham was a man of faith who remained painfully silent. And somewhere between a promise from heaven and a decision made in desperation, a family was torn apart. But the most shocking part of this story is not what Sarah did. It is what God did when everyone else seemed to forget the woman who was suffering.
There is something deeply unsettling about reading a Bible story you have known since childhood and suddenly realizing that you never truly considered the person who suffered the most.
You have heard about Abraham's faith.
You have heard about Sarah's laughter.
You have heard about Isaac, the promised child.
You may even have heard about Ishmael, the son born before the fulfillment of God's promise.
But have you ever stopped long enough to think about Hagar?
Not as a supporting character.
Not as a theological illustration.
Not merely as the mother of Ishmael.
But as a woman.
A real woman with a body, a future, fears, and feelings.
A woman whose life was dramatically changed by decisions made by people who had more power than she did.
And here is the question that should disturb us before we read another verse.
What happens when people who genuinely believe in God begin using other people to accomplish what they think God has promised?
Because that is where this story becomes painfully personal.
And perhaps more uncomfortable than we are prepared to admit.
Sarah was not an unbeliever. Abraham was not an atheist. These were people who had heard from the living God.
Yet genuine faith did not prevent them from making decisions that caused devastating pain.
And if we are willing to read their story without protecting our favorite Bible characters from uncomfortable questions, we may discover something about ourselves.
Something we would rather not confront.
The story begins with a promise.
God had called Abram, later named Abraham, and promised to make him into a great nation. In Genesis 15, God assured him that his own offspring would inherit what had been promised.
Then came the waiting.
Year after year.
No child.
No nursery.
No tiny footsteps.
No fulfillment that Sarah could hold in her arms.
Just an aging couple living beneath a promise that seemed increasingly impossible.
Genesis 16:1 opens with a sentence that carries more sorrow than its simplicity suggests:
"Now Sarai Abram's wife bare him no children." (Genesis 16:1, KJV)
Imagine the weight of those words in a culture where bearing children carried enormous social importance.
Sarah had lived with infertility for years.
She had watched time move forward while her hopes seemed to stand still.
Perhaps she had heard the familiar questions.
When will you have a child?
Perhaps she had seen other women holding babies and felt the ache of wanting something she could not produce.
Scripture does not record all her private thoughts, so we must be careful not to invent them.
But Scripture does reveal her struggle.
And sometimes waiting for God can expose the places where our faith is weakest.
Not because God's promise has failed.
But because our hearts grow tired of waiting.
Then Sarah made a decision.
Genesis 16:2 records her words:
"Behold now, the LORD hath restrained me from bearing: I pray thee, go in unto my maid; it may be that I may obtain children by her."
Read that again.
Not quickly.
Not as a familiar Sunday school passage.
Read it as a human decision with human consequences.
Sarah believed that perhaps the way to obtain the child she desired was through Hagar, her Egyptian servant.
In the ancient Near Eastern world, arrangements involving enslaved women or female servants bearing children for a household were known. Such practices help explain the social setting of Genesis 16.
But understanding a practice historically is not the same as declaring it morally right.
Something can be culturally accepted and still be profoundly harmful.
And this is where the story begins to expose the difference between what people permit and what God desires.
Genesis 16:3 tells us that Sarah took Hagar and gave her to Abraham as a wife.
The Hebrew wording is important.
The text says:
וַתִּקַּח שָׂרַי ... אֶת־הָגָר
Vattiqqaḥ Sarai ... et-Hagar.
"And Sarai took ... Hagar."
Then:
וַתִּתֵּן אֹתָהּ לְאַבְרָם
Vattitten otah le-Avram.
"And she gave her to Abram."
These verbs describe Sarah's actions, not Hagar's freely expressed wishes.
Genesis does not record Hagar being asked for consent.
It does not record her volunteering.
It does not describe her negotiating the arrangement.
It identifies her as Sarah's Egyptian servant, using the Hebrew word שִׁפְחָה (shifchah), a term commonly translated "maidservant" or "female slave."
We should not pretend the text explicitly tells us everything Hagar thought or experienced.
It does not.
But neither should we romanticize a relationship marked by such a serious imbalance of power.
Hagar was not simply a modern surrogate mother entering an independently negotiated agreement.
She was an enslaved or dependent woman within another household's authority.
And the fact that Scripture describes what happened does not mean Scripture endorses what happened.
That distinction matters.
Especially when people use biblical narratives to justify behavior that the narratives themselves may be exposing.
Then comes a sentence that should stop every reader.
"And Abram hearkened to the voice of Sarai." (Genesis 16:2, KJV)
Abraham listened.
The man who had received God's promise participated in the arrangement.
Sarah proposed it.
Abraham agreed to it.
Hagar bore its consequences.
We must be careful not to place the entire moral responsibility on Sarah while treating Abraham as a passive observer.
He was not powerless.
He was a participant.
The Bible does not present this as a command from God.
It was a human decision made in the shadow of a divine promise.
And here is where the story begins to resemble our lives more than we would like.
How often do we pray for something and then become so desperate for an answer that we begin forcing an outcome?
We ask God to restore a relationship, then compromise our convictions because we cannot bear loneliness.
We ask Him to provide, then justify dishonesty because the bills are due.
We ask Him to bless our future, then wound someone in the present because we believe our intentions are good.
We tell ourselves we are being practical.
We tell ourselves we have waited long enough.
We tell ourselves God understands.
But a good desire does not automatically make every method good.
And the fulfillment of God's promise never requires us to abandon God's character.
Faith does not become obedience simply because we attach God's name to our plans.
Hagar became pregnant.
And immediately, the household began to fracture.
Genesis 16:4 says that when Hagar realized she had conceived, her mistress became despised in her eyes.
The text reveals a change in their relationship, though it does not tell us every thought behind Hagar's attitude.
Perhaps pregnancy altered the way Hagar saw her position.
Perhaps resentment had grown.
Perhaps the household's existing tensions became unbearable.
We cannot know everything the narrative leaves unsaid.
But we know what happened next.
Sarah became angry.
And instead of acknowledging the arrangement she herself had proposed, she confronted Abraham.
"My wrong be upon thee." (Genesis 16:5, KJV)
Pain had turned into accusation.
The woman who had wanted a child through Hagar now found herself unable to endure the consequences of her decision.
And Abraham's response is chilling.
"Behold, thy maid is in thy hand; do to her as it pleaseth thee." (Genesis 16:6, KJV)
Think about that.
Hagar had been brought into an arrangement involving Abraham.
She had become pregnant with his child.
And when conflict erupted, Abraham placed her back under Sarah's control.
The Hebrew text then says:
וַתְּעַנֶּהָ שָׂרַי
Vatte'anneha Sarai.
"And Sarai afflicted her."
The verb comes from the Hebrew root ענה (ʿ-n-h), which in this context conveys affliction, harsh treatment, or humiliation.
It is a serious word.
Genesis does not tell us the precise form of every act of mistreatment, so we should not manufacture details.
But the language is strong enough that we should not soften what happened into a harmless domestic disagreement.
Sarah treated Hagar harshly.
And Hagar fled.
A pregnant Egyptian servant ran away into the wilderness.
Away from the household.
Away from the conflict.
Away from the people who had made decisions about her future.
And suddenly the story is no longer just about a promised child.
It is about a suffering woman trying to escape.
Imagine her standing in the wilderness.
Pregnant.
Vulnerable.
Uncertain where she would sleep.
Uncertain whether she would survive.
Uncertain what would happen to her unborn child.
The biblical text does not give us a detailed account of her journey, but it tells us enough to recognize her danger.
And then something extraordinary happens.
Something that changes the way we should read the entire account.
Genesis 16:7 says:
"And the angel of the LORD found her by a fountain of water in the wilderness."
Found her.
Do not rush past those words.
The woman who had been treated as someone else's possession was found by the God who knew her as a person.
She was not lost to Him.
She was not invisible.
She was not outside the reach of His concern.
And then the angel of the LORD spoke.
"Hagar, Sarai's maid, whence camest thou? and whither wilt thou go?" (Genesis 16:8, KJV)
Notice something beautiful and painful at the same time.
He called her Hagar.
By name.
In a narrative where powerful people had repeatedly acted upon her life, God addressed her personally.
He knew who she was.
He knew where she had come from.
And He asked where she was going.
This was not because God needed information.
The question drew Hagar into an encounter in which her suffering was neither overlooked nor treated as irrelevant.
She answered:
"I flee from the face of my mistress Sarai."
No elaborate explanation.
No attempt to make her pain sound impressive.
Just the truth.
She was running from the woman who had mistreated her.
And then we reach one of the most difficult verses in the story.
The angel instructed Hagar to return to Sarah and submit to her authority.
We must not pretend this instruction is emotionally easy.
It is not.
Nor should we turn this particular divine instruction in an ancient narrative into a universal command telling abused people to return to dangerous situations.
Genesis 16 records a specific encounter within a specific redemptive-historical setting.
It does not authorize abuse.
It does not excuse Sarah's mistreatment.
It does not teach that someone experiencing violence must remain in danger.
People facing abuse deserve protection, safety, and appropriate help.
The passage must be read alongside the whole witness of Scripture concerning justice, mercy, and God's concern for the oppressed.
And in this encounter, the command to return was accompanied by a remarkable promise.
The angel told Hagar that her descendants would be multiplied beyond counting.
He also announced that she would bear a son.
And that she must name him Ishmael.
Here the Hebrew becomes breathtaking.
יִשְׁמָעֵאל
Yishmaʿel.
Ishmael.
The name is commonly understood to mean:
"God hears."
Genesis 16:11 explains the reason:
"Because the LORD hath heard thy affliction."
The Hebrew word for "heard" is related to שָׁמַע (shamaʿ), meaning "to hear."
And the word translated "affliction" is עֳנִי (ʿoni), referring to suffering or affliction.
There is a striking connection between the language of Sarah's harsh treatment and the language of Hagar's suffering.
The God who would later hear the cries of Israel under oppression in Egypt was already hearing the affliction of an Egyptian woman in the wilderness.
Consider the reversal.
Hagar was Egyptian.
Later, the descendants of Abraham would suffer under Egyptian oppression.
But here, before the Exodus, an Egyptian woman was suffering inside Abraham's household.
And God heard her.
God's compassion was not restricted by the social boundaries that human beings had constructed.
His attention reached the person others had pushed to the margins.
Then Hagar responded with words unlike anything else in this account.
Genesis 16:13 records:
אַתָּה אֵל רֳאִי
Attah El Ro'i.
Often rendered:
"You are a God of seeing."
Or, more naturally in English:
"You are the God who sees me."
The precise nuance of the Hebrew expression has been discussed by translators and scholars, especially in connection with the explanation that follows.
But the central truth is unmistakable.
Hagar recognized that God had seen her in her distress.
And the place became associated with the name Beer-lahai-roi, commonly understood as "the well of the Living One who sees me," though its exact linguistic interpretation is also discussed.
Pause here.
Because someone reading this has been living like Hagar.
Not necessarily in a wilderness of sand.
But in a wilderness of silence.
You have been the dependable one.
The one who keeps showing up.
The one who carries burdens without telling anyone how heavy they have become.
People notice what you do for them.
But sometimes you wonder whether anyone notices what it costs you.
You smile because explaining your pain would take more energy than you have left.
You pray because you do not know what else to do.
And somewhere beneath all that exhaustion is a question you barely dare to speak.
Does God even see me?
Hagar's story answers with a revelation of God's character.
He sees the afflicted.
He hears the suffering.
He knows the names of those the world overlooks.
But there is something else we must understand.
Being seen by God does not mean every painful circumstance will immediately disappear.
Hagar returned.
Ishmael was born.
And the family story continued.
Years later, God made clear that His covenant promise would be established through a son born to Sarah.
In Genesis 17:19, God announced that Sarah would bear Isaac.
This is important because Genesis 16 must not be reduced to the simplistic claim that Ishmael was merely the product of human failure.
Ishmael was a real child.
A person made in God's image.
And God Himself promised to bless him.
Genesis 17:20 records God's response concerning Ishmael:
"And as for Ishmael, I have heard thee: Behold, I have blessed him, and will make him fruitful, and will multiply him exceedingly."
God's covenant purpose through Isaac did not erase His concern for Ishmael.
That distinction matters.
Because people are not disposable simply because they are not central to a particular covenant promise.
And children are not guilty merely because adults made painful or misguided decisions before they were born.
Then Isaac arrived.
The long-awaited son.
The child whose birth had seemed impossible.
Sarah laughed.
The promise was fulfilled.
We might expect the household to finally settle into peace.
But unresolved pain does not always disappear when a long-awaited blessing arrives.
Sometimes it resurfaces.
Genesis 21 tells us that Sarah saw Ishmael, Hagar's son, laughing or mocking, depending on how the Hebrew is interpreted in context.
The Hebrew verb is related to צחק (tsachaq), the same root associated with Isaac's name and the theme of laughter.
The exact nature of Ishmael's behavior in Genesis 21:9 is debated.
Paul later describes it as persecution in Galatians 4:29, giving a theological interpretation of the conflict.
But we should not invent additional details that Scripture does not provide.
What is clear is Sarah's response.
She demanded that Abraham send Hagar and Ishmael away.
Genesis 21:10 records her words:
"Cast out this bondwoman and her son."
This time Abraham was distressed.
Scripture says the matter was grievous to him because of his son.
God told Abraham to listen to Sarah concerning the covenant line through Isaac, while also promising to make a nation of Ishmael.
This divine assurance must not be confused with a blanket endorsement of every attitude, accusation, or motive within the household.
God was directing His covenant purpose and protecting Ishmael's future, even amid a deeply painful family separation.
Abraham provided bread and water and sent Hagar away.
And once again, Hagar entered the wilderness.
But this time she was not alone.
Her son was with her.
The water ran out.
The situation became desperate.
And Hagar reached a moment no parent wants to imagine.
Genesis 21:16 records her words:
"Let me not see the death of the child."
She sat at a distance.
And wept.
The woman who had once fled because she could no longer endure her suffering now faced the possibility of losing her son.
And here is where the story breaks your heart.
The child who had been named "God hears" was crying in the wilderness.
And God heard him.
Genesis 21:17 says:
"And God heard the voice of the lad."
Then the angel of God called to Hagar from heaven.
"What aileth thee, Hagar? fear not; for God hath heard the voice of the lad where he is."
Where he is.
Not where someone thought he should be.
Not where a family had expected him to remain.
Where he was.
Then God opened Hagar's eyes, and she saw a well of water.
She filled the container.
She gave her son a drink.
And Scripture tells us that God was with the boy as he grew.
What a remarkable testimony.
The God who had seen Hagar in Genesis 16 was still caring for her family in Genesis 21.
The wilderness had not placed them beyond His reach.
And rejection by human beings had not canceled God's concern for them.
Now return to the question that began this story.
Was Sarah wrong to give Hagar to Abraham?
The most responsible biblical answer requires more than a simple condemnation without context.
Genesis does not contain a direct statement saying, "Sarah sinned by giving Hagar to Abraham."
But neither does it present her plan as a divine command or an example believers should imitate.
The arrangement arose from human initiative rather than God's instruction.
It involved an enslaved woman whose consent is not recorded.
It resulted in painful rivalry, harsh treatment, and family division.
And the wider biblical witness establishes God's design for marriage, His concern for justice, and His condemnation of oppression.
Genesis 2:24 describes marriage as a man and his wife becoming one flesh.
Jesus Himself appeals to that creation pattern in Matthew 19:4–6.
So although Scripture records polygamous households, the existence of those arrangements does not make them the creation ideal.
The New Testament also offers a significant interpretation of this story.
Galatians 4:22–31 contrasts Hagar and Sarah in Paul's argument concerning slavery, freedom, law, and promise.
Paul explicitly says he is speaking allegorically in that passage.
His point is about the difference between seeking standing with God through the law and receiving God's promise through Christ.
We must not misuse that allegory to suggest Hagar was morally inferior to Sarah, that Ishmael was less human than Isaac, or that mistreatment was somehow deserved.
The same Bible that uses Hagar within Paul's theological argument also records God personally hearing her affliction and caring for her son.
And Paul writes in Galatians 3:28:
That is not permission to erase the historical differences between people.
It is a declaration that status does not determine a person's standing in Christ.
And here is the uncomfortable truth.
Sarah's story is not merely a warning about impatience.
It is also a warning about what can happen when our desire for a blessing becomes more important to us than the people affected by our pursuit of it.
You can desire something good and still pursue it in a harmful way.
You can be a person of faith and still need repentance.
You can have a genuine calling and still be responsible for the wounds you cause.
And you can be on the receiving end of another person's failure without being abandoned by God.
Perhaps you see yourself in Sarah.
You have waited.
You have been disappointed.
You have tried to take control because trusting God became frightening.
And perhaps your fear led you to decisions that wounded someone else.
The answer is not to excuse yourself because your intentions were sincere.
The answer is repentance.
To confess the truth.
To stop blaming others for what you chose.
To seek forgiveness where possible.
To make restitution where appropriate.
And to trust that God's grace is greater than the failure you finally have the courage to acknowledge.
Perhaps you see yourself in Abraham.
You knew something was wrong, but you remained silent.
You allowed someone else to carry the consequences of a decision you participated in.
You had the influence to intervene.
But you did not.
Then hear this.
Spiritual maturity is not merely believing the right things.
It also requires the courage to do what is right when silence would be easier.
Or perhaps you see yourself in Hagar.
You did not create the situation.
You were caught in decisions made by others.
You were hurt by people who claimed to know God.
And now you are struggling to separate God's character from the behavior of those who represented Him badly.
Please hear this carefully.
The failures of God's people are not the measure of God's goodness.
Sarah's mistreatment was not proof that God approved of cruelty.
Abraham's failures were not proof that God had forgotten justice.
And the suffering Hagar experienced was not evidence that she was worthless.
The Lord saw her.
The Lord heard her.
And the Lord cared for her child.
But even that is not the deepest place this story leads us.
Because centuries later, the God who saw Hagar's affliction revealed His mercy in the person of Jesus Christ.
The eternal Son of God entered our broken world.
He was born into human vulnerability.
He lived among the poor, the overlooked, the grieving, and the rejected.
He touched people others avoided.
He welcomed those society had pushed aside.
He exposed religious hypocrisy.
He confronted sin without treating sinners as beyond the reach of grace.
And then He went to the cross.
Not because humanity had finally become good enough.
But because humanity desperately needed a Savior.
Romans 5:8 declares:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us."
The cross tells us something we must never forget.
God does not save us by pretending sin is harmless.
He saves us through the sacrifice of His Son.
At Calvary, Jesus bore the judgment our sins deserved.
He died.
He was buried.
And on the third day, He rose again.
This is not simply an inspiring ending to a painful story.
This is the Gospel.
And it changes how we understand every human failure recorded in Scripture.
Abraham needed grace.
Sarah needed grace.
Hagar needed God's sustaining mercy.
Ishmael needed God's care.
And we need Jesus Christ.
The great dividing line between the redeemed and the lost is not that some people have made terrible decisions while others have lived perfectly.
"For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God." (Romans 3:23, KJV)
Our hope is not in being better than Sarah.
Our hope is in Christ.
Our righteousness is not established by our ability to defend ourselves.
It is received through faith in the One who died and rose again.
And genuine faith does not leave us comfortable in sin.
It calls us to repentance, forgiveness, obedience, and transformation.
That is why the theme of this ministry matters so deeply.
Not because Jesus changes the historical facts.
Not because He makes every consequence disappear.
Not because repentance erases the pain others have endured.
But because His redeeming power can change the direction of a life that seemed permanently defined by failure.
He can forgive the guilty.
He can heal the wounded.
He can confront the proud.
He can restore the repentant.
He can give hope to those who thought their story was already over.
And if you have been carrying shame for years, remember that forgiveness is not something you purchase by suffering long enough.
It is a gift of God's grace received through faith in Jesus Christ.
Ephesians 2:8–9 says:
"For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast."
You cannot earn salvation by being religious.
You cannot buy forgiveness through donations.
You cannot undo your sins by pretending they never happened.
But you can come to Jesus.
Confess your sins.
Turn from them.
Trust Him.
And receive the mercy that only He can give.
Perhaps the most disturbing part of Sarah and Hagar's story is not that people of faith made terrible mistakes.
It is that we can recognize their mistakes so clearly while remaining blind to our own.
We criticize Sarah's impatience while forcing outcomes in our own lives.
We criticize Abraham's silence while refusing to confront injustice.
We feel compassion for Hagar while overlooking people whose suffering inconveniences us.
And sometimes we speak passionately about God's promises while forgetting the people He commands us to love.
James 1:22 warns:
"But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves."
This story should not merely make us emotional.
It should make us examine our lives.
Who have we wounded while trying to get what we wanted?
Whose pain have we dismissed because acknowledging it would require us to change?
Where have we mistaken our own impatience for God's direction?
And where have we allowed disappointment to become an excuse for disobedience?
These questions are not meant to drive us into hopelessness.
They are meant to bring us to the Savior.
Because conviction without Christ can become despair.
But conviction that leads us to Christ can become the beginning of repentance and renewal.
And maybe that is what someone reading this needs today.
Not another religious performance.
Not another carefully arranged appearance of spiritual strength.
Just the courage to tell God the truth.
Lord, I have been impatient.
Lord, I have hurt people.
Lord, I have been silent when I should have spoken.
Lord, I have been wounded, and I do not know how to heal.
Lord, I have tried to control what I should have entrusted to You.
Lord Jesus, have mercy on me.
You do not need to make that prayer impressive.
You need to mean it.
And if your heart is exhausted, remember Hagar beside the well.
The Lord did not require her to become powerful before He heard her.
He met her in her affliction.
And in Jesus Christ, we have an even greater revelation of the God who sees.
Hebrews 4:15 reminds us that our High Priest is not unable to sympathize with our weaknesses.
Jesus knows human suffering.
He knows betrayal.
He knows rejection.
He knows what it means to be falsely accused and unjustly treated.
And because He is the risen Savior, His compassion is joined to the power to save.
So do not confuse your wilderness with God's absence.
Do not confuse another person's rejection with God's verdict on your worth.
And do not confuse the mistakes of yesterday with the limits of what Christ can do in your life today.
There is still a call to repentance.
There is still grace for the sinner who comes to Jesus.
There is still strength for the weary.
There is still hope for the wounded.
And there is still a Savior who receives those who come to Him.
You can write "Jesus, forgive me" if you recognize a place where you need repentance.
Or write "God sees me" if you have been carrying pain that nobody around you seems to understand.
You do not have to reveal private details or explain painful experiences publicly.
Sometimes a few honest words are enough to let another believer know that you need encouragement.

And if God has brought you through a season when you felt forgotten, consider sharing a brief testimony. Your words may help someone else recognize that their suffering has not placed them beyond God's care.
Please do not let this message end with you.
Not to chase attention.
Not to make yourself look spiritual.
But because there may be a person quietly struggling with shame, impatience, family wounds, or disappointment who needs to encounter the truth of God's Word.
Do not simply accept what you have read here.
Open your Bible.
Examine the Scriptures.
Test every interpretation.
Let God's Word have the final authority.
That is also why Gospel Warrior exists.
We want to help people move beyond surface-level inspiration into serious, Christ-centered discipleship.
Not merely to feel something for a moment.
But to know Scripture, understand the Gospel, grow in discernment, repent where necessary, and become more faithful followers of Jesus Christ.

If you have been blessed by this ministry, consider following Gospel Warrior and inviting your family, friends, fellow believers, struggling Christians, and even those who are still exploring the faith to follow as well.
Every day is another opportunity to encounter Scripture, receive encouragement, confront difficult truths, and point someone toward Christ.
It is not a requirement for salvation.
And it is not a substitute for the biblical responsibilities you have toward your local church, your family, or those in need.
But it can be a meaningful expression of voluntary Christian generosity.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver."
Freely.
Prayerfully.
Without pressure.
Because you believe helping more people encounter the Gospel is a worthwhile mission.
These items are simply practical ways to enjoy or share the ministry's resources. They are not measures of anyone's faith.
The goal is not to place spiritual nourishment behind a paywall.
It is to help make biblical resources available while inviting those who are able and willing to support the ongoing work.
Pray for this ministry.
Invite others to read Scripture.
Encourage someone who is struggling.
Speak about Jesus with humility and courage.
Support faithful Gospel work as God enables you.
Because the mission is bigger than any one page, writer, or ministry.
It belongs to Jesus Christ.
And all the glory must return to Him.
Before you leave, I want you to remember one final scene.
A woman in the wilderness.
A child crying.
An empty water container.
A mother who could no longer bear to watch her son suffer.
And a God who heard.
The story did not end with the household that rejected them.
It continued under the care of the God who had never lost sight of them.
That does not mean every earthly story will resolve the way we hope.
But it does mean that the Lord's faithfulness is not confined to the approval, acceptance, or kindness of other people.
And when we come to Jesus Christ, we encounter the Savior whose grace reaches deeper than our sin and whose mercy is greater than our shame.
Sarah's failures remind us that faith must be accompanied by obedience.
Abraham's failures remind us that spiritual responsibility cannot be abandoned when doing right becomes uncomfortable.
Hagar's suffering reminds us that God sees people whom others overlook.
Ishmael's story reminds us that God's compassion extends beyond the expectations of human beings.
And Jesus Christ reminds us that our deepest hope is not found in the perfection of biblical heroes, but in the perfect Savior to whom the Scriptures ultimately direct us.
So tonight, before you close your Bible, ask yourself one question.
Am I trying to force God to fulfill my plans, or am I surrendering my life to His will?
And if you discover that you have been running, hiding, controlling, blaming, or carrying pain alone, come to Christ.
Not tomorrow.
Not when you finally feel worthy.
Come with repentance.
Come with faith.
Come trusting His mercy.
Because the God who heard Hagar in the wilderness has revealed His saving love through Jesus Christ, who died for sinners and rose again.
And no matter how complicated your story has become, the Gospel still calls you to the One who makes all things new.
You may have been written out of someone else's plans, but you have never been hidden from the eyes of the God who sees.
